about: This prayer was not written for the offertory: it is an old Christmas collect, which the oldest Roman sacramentaries already carry as such. It was brought here and cut open by one insertion — “per hujus aquæ et vini mystérium”, through the mystery of this water and wine. The collect simply asked that we be made sharers in the divinity of him who was made a sharer in our humanity; at the altar the same petition passes through the drop of water poured into the chalice. Hence too the point of the two adverbs: mirabíliter — mirabílius, wonderfully made, more wonderfully restored; the restoring is the greater work of the two. In Masses for the Dead the prayer is said but the water is not blessed.

s01.narrative: The priest lays the host on the corporal and moves to the right side of the altar. He pours wine into the chalice, and blesses with the sign of the cross the water he is about to mix with it.

s02.translation: God, who didst wonderfully make the dignity of human nature and more wonderfully restore it: grant us through the mystery of this water and wine to be sharers in the divinity of him who deigned to be made a partaker of our humanity, Jesus Christ, thy Son, our Lord: who liveth and reigneth with thee in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God: through all ages of ages. Amen.

s03.narrative: In Masses for the Dead the prayer is said, but the water is not blessed — blessings are dropped in those Masses.

w001.function: Vocative; the form is the same as the nominative, because “deus” has no separate vocative.

w002.function: The whole prayer is one sentence: a vocative, a relative clause saying who God is, and only then the petition.

w004.function: A genitive depending on “dignitátem” (w005): the dignity of human nature.

w005.function: One object for two verbs: he made it and he restored it.

w007.function: Cóndere is to found, to establish — the verb for founding cities, not for shaping clay.

w009.function: The comparative of the same adverb as “mirabíliter” (w006). The form doubles as the neuter of the adjective; it is an adverb here because it modifies a verb.

w010.function: A contracted form of reformavísti — liturgical Latin often shortens the perfect this way.

w011.function: Here the petition begins; everything before it was invocation.

w014.function: It governs the water and the wine together; the form marks no gender and the two nouns are of different genders, so none is claimed here.

w018.function: Accusative after “per” (w013). These are the only words by which the offertory enlarged the Christmas Collect.

w019.function: A genitive depending on “divinitátis” (w020); its masculine gender comes from its referent, Christ, who is named only a few words later.

w021.function: The infinitive is the object of “da” (w011): grant us to be.

w022.function: The form is nominative as well as accusative; accusative, because the understood subject of “esse” (w021) is an accusative us, not the dative “nobis” (w012). Con-sors is one who shares another's lot (sors).

w023.function: The second relative clause turns the first around: we share his divinity because he took a share in our humanity.

w024.function: A genitive with “párticeps” (w029), just as “divinitátis” (w020) goes with “consórtes” (w022).

w026.function: The infinitive of fio — the verb that serves Latin as the passive of “to make”: fíeri means to become, to be made.

w028.function: With “dignátus” (w027) it makes one past-tense form of a deponent verb; on its own it means nothing here.

w029.function: Predicate after “fíeri” (w026). Pars-cápere: one who takes a part.

w035.function: This whole file of nouns is one apposition to “qui” (w023) — the name at last spoken.

w036.function: Here begins the closing formula, the same in every collect addressed to the Father through the Son.

w037.function: One written word carrying two: the preposition cum stands after the pronoun, as it always does with the personal pronouns (mecum, nobíscum).

w045.function: Nominative, not vocative like “Deus” (w001): apposition to “Qui” (w036) — he who lives and reigns as God.

w049.function: A Hebrew idiom rendered word for word: ages of ages simply means for ever.
